claims.text: RoleBindings, NetworkPolicies and ResourceQuotas/LimitRanges are namespaced objects; the Pod Security admission level is set per namespace by its pod-security.kubernetes.io labels.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Using RBAC Authorization > RoleBinding; Network Policies; Pod Security Admission > namespace labels; Resource Quotas; Limit Ranges

claims.text: CustomResourceDefinitions, ClusterRoles and Nodes are cluster-scoped: one definition for the whole cluster, shared by every namespace; all namespaces share the API server and etcd, and Pods on one node share that node's kernel.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Namespaces > Not all objects are in a namespace; Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions (scope); Cluster Architecture

claims.text: A ResourceQuota with hard requests.cpu, requests.memory and pods caps the sum of CPU/memory requests and the number of non-terminal Pods in its namespace; the API server rejects a create that would exceed it with 403 Forbidden and a message containing 'exceeded quota'.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Resource Quotas > Compute Resource Quota; Object Count Quota

claims.text: Quota is enforced at admission (the ResourceQuota admission controller) when an object is created; it is checked against requests, not measured usage, and it does not slow, evict or stop Pods already running.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Resource Quotas (enforced on creation; changes to quota do not affect already created resources); Admission Controllers > ResourceQuota

claims.text: A Deployment's Pods are created by its ReplicaSet; when the API server refuses a Pod for quota, the ReplicaSet controller records a FailedCreate event on the ReplicaSet and retries; the refused Pod does not exist (not Pending); kubectl scale itself succeeds.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: ReplicaSet; Resource Quotas; team-quota.sh lines 27-29 comments and outputs/stage-4/scripts/k8s/team-quota.txt lines 10-18 @ stage-4

claims.text: If a quota covers requests.cpu or requests.memory, every new Pod must set requests or limits for them (requests default from limits), or the API server refuses it ('must specify requests.cpu').
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Resource Quotas > Compute Resource Quota (requests must be specified); outputs/stage-4/scripts/k8s/team-quota.txt line 21

claims.text: A LimitRange of type Container with defaultRequest and default writes those requests and limits into containers that set none, at Pod creation (LimitRanger admission), before the ResourceQuota admission check, so the quota counts the defaults.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Limit Ranges; Admission Controllers > LimitRanger, ResourceQuota (mutating before validating); team-limit-range.yaml lines 1-5 @ stage-4

claims.text: The ResourceQuota counts compute requests and Pods here; it does not limit how many calls a namespace's clients make to the API server, so one team's overload of the API server can slow other namespaces too.
claims.source_hint: Kubernetes docs: Resource Quotas (types of quota); API Priority and Fairness (fair queuing limits, not removes, the effect); team-quota.yaml lines 17-20 @ stage-4

Without a NetworkPolicy, Pods accept connections from Pods in every namespace; a namespace alone does not limit who changes what; a CPU limit (not a quota) slows a container using more CPU; a Pod whose requests fit no node stays Pending with an event such as Insufficient cpu.

claims.text: ADR 0012 @ stage-4: Đơn Hàng serves several shops, one shared deployment for all: a shop is data inside the system, opening a shop adds data and is not a deploy (CH-2), isolation is built inside the system; one copy of the system per shop was an option not chosen.

Opinion: when teams belong to one company and trust each other, sharing one cluster through namespaces with their own bindings, policies, Pod Security level, quota and LimitRange fits; tenants that must neither affect nor see each other need more than namespaces.
claims.source_hint: trade-off reasoning; Kubernetes docs: Multi-tenancy (soft vs hard multi-tenancy)

claims.text: Opinion: when teams need CRD versions that conflict, namespaces cannot separate them (one CRD per cluster): agree on one version or run separate clusters; a namespace alone cannot promise machines free of other workloads: by default Pods share nodes and their kernel.
